title: The weight of harsh words and the athlete's unfinished contest
english: The horsemen formed three companies against us and surrounded the camels. So the devil made the camels fall under the horsemen, the donkeys and the yokes of oxen under the captors, and the sheep he hated; for this reason he brought down fire on them. But he also plotted against the sons, and he sought an opportunity to destroy them. If he had found them reading, he would not have touched the house, nor would he have had a place to kill them; if he had found them praying, he could have done nothing against them. But when he found an opportunity, he prevailed. What was the opportunity? It was drunkenness; it was a drinking party. And note that the spirit touched the corners of the house: at the street corners the hypocrites stand and pray. Everyone who has not mounted the straight road uses the corners, and a broad corner is abundant and slack wickedness.

Chapter 19. "How long will you make my soul weary?" Just as heavy bodies placed on the bodies of animals make the bearers grow tired, so there are certain heavy words which, when someone hears them, make him weary, as if pressed down by the weight of the words' power—words spoken reproachfully and harshly, or for abuse. So now, when Job felt the words spoken by Bildad as a heavy burden, he grew weary in soul and says: "How long will you make my soul weary, and weigh down your words against me like a heavy burden?" You see that the words of the tyrant of the Shuhites are tyrannical, which Job heard and speaks the words set before us. For nothing else strikes the soul of a human being the way a harsh word does. Often someone has endured tortures inflicted on the body but has not endured words. Yet the perfect athlete, even if he grows weary, still endures harsh words. To endure insult belongs to a great man. Therefore the Apostle says among his brave deeds: "When reviled, we bless; when slandered, we entreat" (1 Corinthians 4:12). And now Job is the noblest of athletes, the one saying these things. His book contains nothing else in particular but his courage and his endurance. But still he feels the weariness he has grown weary with from the harsh word of those who came to visit him. And since the heaviness of the word, like a burden placed on the soul, makes it grow weary, for this reason he says: Why, friends, do you add the pain of the soul to the body's agonies, pricking more with your words than the sufferings prick the body?

"You speak against me." Often someone speaks against another by doing evil; but when he becomes shameless, he speaks to that person's face, not refuting, not speaking the truth, but reproaching and insulting. "I will cry out, and nowhere is judgment." Now if I cry out, my judgment nowhere comes; I am still contending. It is as if he said: Like an athlete in the stadium I have cried out, and nowhere does my judgment arise; for I am still wrestling. If I do not finish the wrestling bout, the judgment of the crown does not come. And I say these things so that we do not accuse God, because Job suffers so much and nowhere is judgment—that is, the judgment of freedom and release from terrible things.

Chapter 20. "If his gifts go up to heaven." The heretic too, when he prays, when his sacrifice goes up with lofty speech, when he seems to be firmly established, then he will finally be destroyed; for his prayer is reckoned to him as sin. But we church members who know his errors will say: Where are such people, dreaming and fashioning errors for themselves? They do not fix their mind on the truth, and so they go astray; and they become like a dream that has flown away, which will not be found. David sings something like this: "The enemies of the Lord have failed; as soon as they were glorified and exalted, failing like smoke they failed" (Psalm 37:20); and again: "Like a dream when one awakes" (Psalm 73:20).
